propositions.text: The applicant is a 27-year-old Indian citizen who came to Canada in 2019 on a study permit for a two-year diploma.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a 27-year-old citizen of India. She first came to Canada in September 2019 on a study permit to pursue a two-year Chemical Laboratory Technician Diploma at Sheridan College.

propositions.text: The applicant's study permit expired in July 2023 after several extensions and she lost full-time student status.
propositions.quote: After several extensions, the applicant’s study permit expired in July 2023. During the latter part of her studies, for various reasons, the applicant was unable to maintain her status as a full-time student.

propositions.text: Her post-graduate work permit application was refused due to loss of full-time student status.
propositions.quote: As a result, when she applied for a post-graduate work permit (PGWP), the application was refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a 27-year-old Indian who lost full-time student status and had her post-graduate work permit refused.

propositions.text: In August 2024, the applicant applied for a temporary resident permit and an open work permit to gain Canadian work experience.
propositions.quote: In August 2024, the applicant applied for a temporary resident permit (TRP) under subsection 24(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA). At the same time, she also requested an open work permit.

propositions.text: The applicant explained she sought a TRP to overcome PGWP ineligibility and obtain Canadian work experience.
propositions.quote: The applicant explained that she was seeking a TRP to overcome her ineligibility for a PGWP because she wanted to obtain Canadian work experience.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant applied for a TRP and open work permit to gain Canadian work experience, as she explained.

propositions.text: The officer refused the application because a TRP was not justified without sufficient documentation of difficulty returning home to regularize status.
propositions.quote: In particular, the officer found that the applicant had not provided “sufficient documentation to prove that [she] would experience difficulty should [she] be expected to return to [her] home country in order to regularize [her] status, and re-apply for a [work permit].”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused the TRP application for lack of sufficient documentation proving difficulty returning home to regularize status.

propositions.text: The applicant seeks judicial review of the decision as unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant seeks judicial review of this decision under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA on the basis that the decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded to interfere with the decision.
propositions.quote: As I will explain, I am not persuaded that there is any basis to interfere with the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant seeks judicial review as unreasonable; the court is not persuaded to interfere with the decision.

propositions.text: The merits of the officer’s decision are reviewed on a reasonableness standard per Vavilov 2019 SCC 65.
propositions.quote: The parties agree, as do I, that the merits of the officer’s decision should be reviewed on a reasonableness standard (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 10).

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov, at para 85).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the reasonableness standard from Vavilov applies, requiring coherent, justified decisions.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires a 'reasons first' approach examining the decision maker’s justification holistically and contextually.
propositions.quote: When conducting reasonableness review, a reviewing court must take a “reasons first” approach that examines and evaluates the justification the administrative decision maker has given for its decision, always bearing in mind the history of the proceeding and the administrative context in which the decision was made (Mason v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 at paras 58-60).

propositions.text: The decision must be read in light of evidence, party submissions, policies, and past decisions.
propositions.quote: The reviewing court must read the decision maker’s reasons “holistically and contextually” (Vavilov, at para 97) and in light of “the evidence before the decision maker, the submissions of the parties, publicly available policies or guidelines that informed the decision maker’s work, and past decisions of the relevant administrative body” (Vavilov, at para 94).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness review requires holistic, contextual reading of reasons with evidence and policies.

propositions.text: To set aside a decision as unreasonable, serious shortcomings must exist undermining justification, intelligibility, and transparency.
propositions.quote: To set aside a decision on the basis that it is unreasonable, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov, at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states that serious shortcomings are required to set aside a decision as unreasonable.

propositions.text: Subsection 24(1) IRPA allows TRPs for inadmissible persons if justified in the circumstances to avoid undue hardship.
propositions.quote: Subsection 24(1) of the IRPA provides that an officer may issue a TRP to a foreign national who is inadmissible to Canada or who does not meet the requirements of the Act if the officer is of the opinion that doing so “is justified in the circumstances.”

propositions.text: The provision aims to provide flexibility to avoid undue hardship despite inadmissibility or non-compliance.
propositions.quote: It is well established that the objective of this provision is to provide flexibility in situations where a strict application of the IRPA would result in undue hardship because there are compelling reasons to allow a foreign national to enter or remain in Canada despite their inadmissibility or non-compliance with the Act: see Farhat v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1275 at para 22; and Ogbonna v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 1467 at paras 19-29.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 24(1) IRPA allows TRPs to avoid undue hardship despite inadmissibility, citing precedent.

propositions.text: The officer reasonably concluded the applicant did not establish a compelling reason for a TRP.
propositions.quote: In my view, it was open to the officer to conclude that the applicant had not established that issuing a TRP was justified in the circumstances.

propositions.text: The burden was on the applicant to show a compelling reason to remain despite inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: The burden was on the applicant to demonstrate that she had a compelling reason to be allowed to remain in Canada despite her inadmissibility.

propositions.text: The officer found no evidence the applicant would experience difficulty regularizing status from India.
propositions.quote: Critically, the officer found that a TRP was not justified because the applicant could regularize her status from India and she had not provided any evidence that she would “experience difficulty” if she were required to do so.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the officer improperly applied a hardship-based test.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the applicant that the officer has imported some sort of hardship-based test.

propositions.text: The officer considered whether a compelling need for a TRP existed given other viable options for work experience.
propositions.quote: Rather, the officer was simply considering whether there was a compelling need for a TRP given that other options for achieving the outcome the applicant sought – the ability to obtain work experience in Canada – were reasonably open to the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer reasonably required a compelling reason for a TRP and did not apply a hardship test as the applicant alleges.

propositions.text: The officer’s reasons were brief but clear and justified given the applicant had other viable options.
propositions.quote: While the officer’s analysis is somewhat cursory, the central point is clear: since the applicant had not demonstrated that she did not have other viable options for obtaining Canadian work experience, she had not demonstrated a compelling reason to be allowed to remain in Canada on a TRP in order to obtain that experience.

propositions.text: No further explanation was needed as the TRP application was determinatively refused.
propositions.quote: Since this was determinative of the TRP application, there was no need for the officer to say more about why a TRP was not justified in the circumstances.

propositions.text: The officer’s reasons are transparent, intelligible, and justified when read in context.
propositions.quote: The officer’s reasons are brief but they are transparent and intelligible. Most importantly, when read in the context of the record before the officer, the statutory requirements, and the governing jurisprudence, they justify the result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer’s brief reasons transparent, intelligible, and justified given the applicant’s other options.

propositions.text: The applicant’s circumstances are sympathetic but do not make the decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s circumstances are sympathetic and her desire to obtain work experience in Canada is understandable. While she must have been disappointed by the officer’s decision, she has not demonstrated that it is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review must, therefore, be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant’s circumstances sympathetic but dismisses the judicial review as the decision is not unreasonable.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance arise for certification under IRPA s 74(d).
propositions.quote: The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that no question arises.

propositions.text: The judicial review is dismissed and no question of general importance is stated.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is stated.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review and finds no question of general importance for certification.
